scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Gusadi dance is deeply rooted in the cultural practices of the Raj Gond tribes.
It is traditionally performed during the Dandari festival, which is considered a key cultural and religious event for the tribal communities.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed during the annual Dandari festival, lasting five to nine days around Diwali.
It serves as a religious devotion to deities like Padmalpuri Kako Etmasur and as a social mechanism for courtship and matchmaking between villages.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance follows a defined set of seven moves known as the Edum Chaal.

These include the Sur Chaal (introductory greeting), Gussadi Chaal (bending and rhythmic movement), Mahadevana Chaal (spiritual movement), Urum Chaal (mimicking a monitor lizard), Hedge Chaal (mimicking a bear), an animal-themed move, and the concluding Sakshi Chaal, which involves rapid spinning and a final high jump.
Watch for Urum Chaal, Hedge Chaal.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Dancers move in lines and travel between villages.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is driven by tribal instruments including the Thudum (a large drum used to signal arrival), the parra, the vette, and the kodal.
Listen for the Thudum, parra, vette, kodal.
The music is defined by the deep, resonant sound of the Thudum drum, which signals the arrival of the troupe, accompanied by the rhythmic beat of parra, vette, and kodal instruments.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear the Malpuve, a large hat made of over a thousand peacock feathers.
They apply ash to their bodies, wear fake beards and mustaches, and dress in saffron or yellow clothing with goat or deer skin at the waist.
They carry a wooden stick called a Gangaram Sota.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Kanaka Raju (1941–2024) is the most famous practitioner, known as the 'Gussadi King.' He performed at the Red Fort in 1982 and received the Padma Shri in 2021 for his contributions to the dance.
The dance is primarily practiced in the Adilabad District of Telangana and parts of Maharashtra.
The dance is passed down through the Raj Gond tribal communities, with elders and experienced dancers like Kanaka Raju serving as primary instructors.
